title: Alternate Key
description: Preserve independent candidate identities after primary-key selection, implement required alternate uniqueness, and distinguish optional unique values from classical keys.
notes:
## Another valid way to identify the same fact

An alternate key is a candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key. Suppose Course has an internal course_id and a required institutional course_code. If each independently identifies the course under the documented rules, both are candidate keys. Choosing course_id as primary leaves course_code as an alternate key. The course code does not lose its identifying guarantee merely because a different key received the primary designation.

The word alternate describes its role, not weaker enforcement. An alternate identifier can be important to students, administrators, imported files, and reports. If two rows claim the same institutional course code while policy says it identifies one course, the data is inconsistent even when the rows have different internal primary identifiers. The surrogate primary key alone cannot prevent that business-identity collision.

## Establish candidate status before naming an alternate

A field is not an alternate key merely because it looks useful for searching. Candidate-key status requires a guaranteed identifying set and minimality. A course title can repeat across departments or years, so a current collection of unique titles does not establish an alternate identity. An indexed search field can be useful without being a key at all.

Likewise, an email address may be optional, shared, mutable, or compared under particular rules. A system can intentionally require unique nonmissing institutional email addresses, but those assumptions must be explicit. Do not promote any convenient descriptive field to alternate-key status solely because its current sample values differ. The allowed-state contract, not the visual appearance of a column, supplies the guarantee.

## SQL needs uniqueness and an absence policy

A required alternate identity commonly uses UNIQUE with NOT NULL. UNIQUE prevents conflicting ordinary values or combinations, while NOT NULL requires the identifying information to be present. A primary key supplies its own required-key-component behaviour; the alternate declaration should express the relevant obligations without assuming the two keywords are interchangeable in every detail.

```sql
CREATE TABLE courses (
  course_id INT PRIMARY KEY,
  course_code VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  course_title VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL
);
```

This definition permits two courses with the same title if their identities differ. It rejects a repeated course_code even when course_id changes. It also rejects a missing required course code. These are separate acceptance cases, and each should be checked directly rather than treating one successful insert as evidence that the complete alternate identity policy works.

## Optional uniqueness is a different contract

An optional external reference can be required to be distinct when present while allowing many rows with no value yet. MySQL's nullable UNIQUE behaviour can fit that contract. It does not provide a definite nonmissing identifier for every tuple, so it should not be described uncritically as a classical candidate key for the whole relation.

Consider an optional library barcode assigned after a physical copy arrives. Several planned copies may have NULL barcodes, while every assigned barcode must be unique. That is a useful optional uniqueness rule. If the application needs to identify every planned copy before barcodes arrive, a different required identifier is needed. Do not infer that absent barcodes magically distinguish the pending copies from one another.

## Alternate identities can be composite

An alternate key can contain several attributes. A course can have a required department_code and local_course_code whose combination is unique, while course_id remains primary. Different departments can reuse the same local code, and a department can offer several courses. The pair can identify a course even though neither component identifies it alone.

Declare one combined UNIQUE constraint for the pair rather than separate uniqueness constraints on both components. Separate constraints would forbid legitimate department participation and code reuse. Minimality still matters: if local_course_code is already globally unique by policy, adding department_code is redundant and the pair is a nonminimal superkey rather than another candidate key under that stronger policy.

## Compare according to the intended identifier rules

String uniqueness follows applicable type and collation rules. If course codes differing only in letter case should represent the same identifier, the contract should say so and the implementation should enforce that choice. If they must be distinct, that is a different comparison requirement. Do not assume displayed spellings correspond to distinct database identities under every default collation.

Normalization in an input pipeline can also change which values reach the database. Trimming or case folding may be intentional, but it should match how imports, forms, and lookups interpret the identifier. A required uniqueness constraint protects stored values under its comparison rules; it does not automatically validate the external issuing authority or reconstruct distinctions discarded before storage.

## Lookups can use the alternate identity

Users may know a course by code while applications join its related facts using course_id. A lookup can resolve the required unique code to the internal identity and descriptive title. The two identifiers can coexist without forcing every screen to display internal numbers. Make the lookup predicate and selected result clear so repeated titles do not create ambiguity.

```sql
SELECT course_id, course_title
FROM courses
WHERE course_code = 'DB101';
```

Under the declared required unique code policy, this returns at most one course. It can return no rows if the code is absent. Do not select the first matching title and assume it is equivalent: titles are descriptive and may repeat. A valid lookup follows the actual alternate identity rather than a convenient approximate label.

## Foreign references can target supported alternate keys

A foreign key can reference an appropriate unique alternate key where the database supports the required definition. The columns, types, ordering, index requirements, and referential actions must be compatible. It is inaccurate to state that every possible UNIQUE column in every dialect is automatically an acceptable target without checking those conditions.

The chosen reference has lifecycle consequences. A business course code might change while the internal course identity stays stable. Referencing the code can require coordinated updates or an explicit supported action when it changes. Referencing the internal identifier can decouple that change from related facts. Neither choice is universally correct; the actual public identifier contract and update policy determine the appropriate design.

## Existing data must fit a new guarantee

Before adding an alternate uniqueness rule, audit repeated proposed values and missing required identifiers. A sample with no duplicates is weaker than an audit of the complete relevant dataset. Existing conflicts need a deliberate interpretation: are they duplicate records, reused codes, distinct historical editions, or evidence that the proposed identity is not actually unique under the business model?

Do not delete arbitrary rows to make a constraint fit a mistaken assumption. A course code reused across academic years might require a year component or a revised identity policy. The appropriate resolution follows fact meaning and caller dependencies. A local exercise can begin with compatible data, while a real migration needs authorized investigation and a transition that preserves legitimate information.

## Test alternate enforcement independently

Try a new internal primary identifier with an existing alternate value. It should fail under the required uniqueness contract. Also test a valid distinct alternate value with a repeated descriptive title; that should pass. A separate missing-value case verifies the required absence policy. These cases isolate the alternate rule from the primary rule instead of causing every failure through the primary identifier alone.

A lookup by only one component of a composite alternate identity can return several courses. Supply the whole identifying combination when the task requires one course. For a composite alternate identity, test repeated individual components with distinct complete pairs, then challenge the exact pair. Record what the database actually rejected and why. Local scratch checks establish the exercised behaviour on the recorded engine, while exact provider behaviour, reference transitions, and production authorization remain separate verification concerns. Alternate keys are useful when these independent identifying promises stay visible, enforced, and aligned with the facts they represent.

questions.question_text: What is an alternate key?
options: A foreign key that references a different table
A candidate key that was not chosen as the primary key
A key made of alternating data types
A key that changes value periodically
questions.explanation: Alternate key = candidate key minus whichever one became the primary key.

questions.question_text: How is an alternate key typically implemented in SQL?
options: With the PRIMARY KEY keyword
With UNIQUE and an appropriate NOT NULL policy for a required candidate identity
With a FOREIGN KEY constraint
It cannot be enforced in SQL at all
questions.explanation: A required alternate candidate identity needs both uniqueness and nonmissing values; optional uniqueness is a different contract.

questions.question_text: In MySQL, does a plain nullable UNIQUE column forbid NULL like a primary key?
options: Yes, identically
No; nullable UNIQUE permits NULL, including multiple absent values under MySQL rules
UNIQUE forbids exactly one NULL value
UNIQUE converts NULLs to zero automatically
questions.explanation: The absence policy must be specified separately. Ordinary NULL inequality is not the explanation for a TRUE comparison.

questions.question_text: How many alternate keys can a table have?
options: Exactly one, always
Zero, one, or many, depending on how many unchosen candidate keys exist
Exactly the same number as foreign keys
Alternate keys are not allowed in SQL
questions.explanation: There can be zero or more unchosen candidate keys after selecting one primary candidate.

questions.question_text: Can a foreign key in another table reference an alternate key instead of the primary key?
options: Never, under any circumstances
Yes, when the alternate unique key and referencing definition satisfy the target engine’s requirements
Only if the alternate key is also the primary key
Only in NoSQL databases
questions.explanation: Alternate unique keys can be supported reference targets, subject to actual engine, type, index and definition requirements.

questions.question_text: If students has candidate keys {id} and {email}, and {id} is the primary key, what is {email}?
options: A foreign key
An alternate key
A super key only, not a candidate key
An invalid key with no formal name
questions.explanation: Since {email} was a candidate key that wasn't chosen as primary, it's specifically an alternate key.

questions.question_text: Why can an optional distinct-when-present SQL identifier use nullable UNIQUE, while remaining different from a required classical alternate key?
options: It never makes sense and is always a bug
Some rows may legitimately not have that optional value yet (e.g. an email not yet collected), while any values that ARE present must still be distinct
NULL values are required by the SQL standard for all UNIQUE columns
UNIQUE columns cannot hold real data at all
questions.explanation: Optional uniqueness can be useful, but it does not provide a nonmissing identifier for every row.

questions.question_text: Is it accurate to say an alternate key is 'less enforced' than a primary key?
options: Yes, alternate keys are only a suggestion, not enforced
No; supported UNIQUE enforcement is real, while the chosen primary role and nullability policy remain distinct
Alternate keys are enforced only during INSERT, never UPDATE
Alternate keys are enforced only in application code, never the database
questions.explanation: The uniqueness aspect is enforced rather than advisory; an alternate key can also be a supported foreign-key target.

questions.question_text: Does choosing course_id as primary invalidate a guaranteed candidate course_code?
options: Yes; all other candidates disappear
No; course_code remains an alternate key
Only title remains a key
It becomes a foreign key automatically
questions.explanation: Primary choice preserves other candidate identities.

questions.question_text: Why does a distinct internal id not make a repeated required course_code acceptable?
options: Primary keys disable all UNIQUE checks
Titles determine every code
The alternate identity has its own uniqueness obligation
A larger id repairs the code
questions.explanation: Independent identifying rules must both hold.

questions.question_text: Which write directly challenges alternate course_code uniqueness?
options: An existing course_id with a new code only
A shared title with distinct identities
A new course_id with an existing course_code
A missing query alias
questions.explanation: The failure should arise from the alternate rule, not only the primary key.

questions.question_text: Can a composite alternate identity permit local code reuse across departments?
options: No; every component must be globally unique
Only if no primary key exists
Only if names are unique
Yes; the complete department-code pair is unique
questions.explanation: The combined identity differs from component uniqueness.

questions.question_text: Why does nullable UNIQUE not identify every pending record with missing values?
options: Several records can lack that optional identifier
NULL automatically creates different numbers
Each missing value is a definite email
A display label supplies uniqueness
questions.explanation: Optional absence is not a complete required identity.

questions.question_text: What can a course-code lookup return under a required unique code rule?
options: Exactly one row for every possible string
At most one matching course
Every repeated course title
One row per department always
questions.explanation: Uniqueness limits matches, while absent codes return none.

questions.question_text: What affects whether differently cased string codes collide?
options: Only the font
Only the row count
The intended comparison policy and column collation
Only the SQL alias
questions.explanation: Stored string uniqueness follows applicable comparison rules.

questions.question_text: Why audit code reuse across academic years before declaring global uniqueness?
options: Every reused code is necessarily a duplicate person
UNIQUE always deletes history
Years cannot be attributes
The intended fact identity may include a year or edition
questions.explanation: Existing patterns can reveal a mistaken proposed business identity.

questions.question_text: Does an index used for searching a title make title an alternate key?
options: No; search usefulness does not guarantee minimal unique identity
Yes; every index is an alternate key
Only for text columns
Only for sorted output
questions.explanation: Indexing and candidate-key status are distinct.

questions.question_text: What should be checked before referencing an alternate key?
options: Only its displayed position
Supported target-key, type, index and lifecycle requirements
Only the shortest spelling
Only whether it contains digits
questions.explanation: Reference compatibility and change policy matter.

questions.question_text: What should remain valid if course titles are descriptive?
options: Two rows claiming the same required course_code
A missing mandatory code
Two courses with the same title and distinct required identities
Two primary-key declarations
questions.explanation: Descriptive repetition is not an identity conflict.

questions.question_text: What does isolated alternate-constraint execution establish?
options: Every provider configuration
All production reference transitions
External identifier issuance truth
The checked accepted and rejected cases on the recorded engine
questions.explanation: The evidence does not exceed its exercised scope.

coding_problems.title: Resolve a course through its alternate identity
coding_problems.task: Return course_id and course_title for the required unique course_code DB101. Repeated titles do not identify a course.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE courses (course_id INT PRIMARY KEY, course_code VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL UNIQUE, course_title VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL);
constraints: Codes are canonical uppercase strings; the lookup matches the exact supplied code.
edge_cases: The requested code can be absent.
Other courses can share the title.
hints: Filter by course_code rather than course_title.
The alternate uniqueness rule limits the result population.
coding_problems.solution_sql: SELECT course_id, course_title FROM courses WHERE course_code = 'DB101';
coding_problems.explanation: The lookup uses the independent alternate identity while returning the selected internal identity and description.

coding_problems.title: Keep an alternate course identity enforced
coding_problems.task: courses already has course_id as primary key and required course_code values. Add UNIQUE(course_code) named course_code_identity, then return course_id, course_code and course_title. Permit repeated titles but reject repeated codes even under a new primary id.
coding_problems.starter_sql: -- Add the course_code_identity uniqueness constraint, then return the course facts.
coding_problems.schema_sql: CREATE TABLE courses (course_id INT PRIMARY KEY, course_code VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, course_title VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL);
coding_problems.expected:
course_id	course_code	course_title
1	DB101	Databases
2	DB201	Databases
constraints: Initial codes are unique and nonmissing.
edge_cases: Different primary identities can still conflict on alternate identity.
Required alternate identity cannot be absent.
hints: The table already has a primary key; do not declare another.
Use a separate UNIQUE constraint for the alternate guarantee.
coding_problems.solution_sql:
ALTER TABLE courses ADD CONSTRAINT course_code_identity UNIQUE (course_code);
SELECT course_id, course_code, course_title FROM courses ORDER BY course_id;
coding_problems.explanation: The added constraint protects an independent required identity without imposing uniqueness on descriptive titles.

original_questions.question_text: How is an alternate key typically implemented in SQL?
options: With the PRIMARY KEY keyword
With a UNIQUE constraint
With a FOREIGN KEY constraint
It cannot be enforced in SQL at all
original_questions.explanation: SQL reserves PRIMARY KEY for the chosen key; alternate keys are enforced with UNIQUE.

original_questions.question_text: Does a UNIQUE constraint by itself forbid NULL values the same way PRIMARY KEY does?
options: Yes, identically
No — most engines allow multiple NULLs in a UNIQUE column, since NULL is not considered equal to another NULL
UNIQUE forbids exactly one NULL value
UNIQUE converts NULLs to zero automatically
original_questions.explanation: This is the key SQL-level difference: UNIQUE alone doesn't imply NOT NULL, and NULLs aren't compared as duplicates of each other.

original_questions.question_text: How many alternate keys can a table have?
options: Exactly one, always
Zero, one, or many, depending on how many unchosen candidate keys exist
Exactly the same number as foreign keys
Alternate keys are not allowed in SQL
original_questions.explanation: Unlike primary key (always exactly one), a table can have any number of alternate keys, including zero.

original_questions.question_text: Can a foreign key in another table reference an alternate key instead of the primary key?
options: Never, under any circumstances
Most SQL dialects technically allow referencing any UNIQUE column, though referencing the primary key is far more common
Only if the alternate key is also the primary key
Only in NoSQL databases
original_questions.explanation: It's technically possible in most dialects, though primary-key references are the conventional, more maintainable default.

original_questions.question_text: If students has candidate keys {id} and {email}, and {id} is the primary key, what is {email}?
options: A foreign key
An alternate key
A super key only, not a candidate key
An invalid key with no formal name
original_questions.explanation: Since {email} was a candidate key that wasn't chosen as primary, it's specifically an alternate key.

original_questions.question_text: Why might allowing multiple NULLs in a UNIQUE alternate-key column actually make business sense?
options: It never makes sense and is always a bug
Some rows may legitimately not have that optional value yet (e.g. an email not yet collected), while any values that ARE present must still be distinct
NULL values are required by the SQL standard for all UNIQUE columns
UNIQUE columns cannot hold real data at all
original_questions.explanation: For an optional-but-must-be-distinct-when-present attribute, allowing multiple NULLs (absent values) while still enforcing distinctness among the real values is exactly the desired behavior.

original_questions.question_text: Is it accurate to say an alternate key is 'less enforced' than a primary key?
options: Yes, alternate keys are only a suggestion, not enforced
No — a UNIQUE constraint is fully enforced by the database; it's simply not the table's designated primary/foreign-key-target identifier
Alternate keys are enforced only during INSERT, never UPDATE
Alternate keys are enforced only in application code, never the database
original_questions.explanation: UNIQUE constraints are just as strictly enforced by the database as PRIMARY KEY's uniqueness aspect — the difference is role, not enforcement strength.
